practices.title: Empty catch block swallows exceptions
practices.description: Catching an exception and doing nothing hides failures until they surface somewhere confusing much later, instead of at the point they actually happened.
practices.risk: Data corruption or a broken downstream call goes unnoticed; the bug report that eventually comes in points nowhere near the real cause.

practices.title: Catching generic Exception instead of a specific type
practices.description: Catching Exception or Throwable masks unrelated failures, including unchecked bugs like a NullPointerException, as if they were the expected failure mode.
practices.risk: A real bug (NPE, ClassCastException) gets silently absorbed by handling meant for an expected, recoverable failure like a missing file.

practices.title: Losing the original exception cause when wrapping
practices.description: Wrapping an exception in a new one without passing the original as the cause discards the stack trace that shows what actually failed.
practices.risk: Production incident logs show only the wrapper's generic message; diagnosing the real failure requires reproducing it from scratch.

practices.title: Throwing a generic RuntimeException with a vague message
practices.description: A bare RuntimeException("Error") tells the caller and the operator nothing about what went wrong or how to react to it.
practices.risk: An on-call engineer paged at 3am sees only 'Error' in the stack trace and has to read the surrounding code to find out what actually failed.

practices.title: Catching NullPointerException or ClassCastException as control flow
practices.description: NullPointerException and ClassCastException almost always indicate a programming bug, not an expected condition to branch on.
practices.risk: The actual bug (why the reference was null) is hidden behind a catch block that treats the crash as normal, so it never gets fixed and can resurface with worse consequences elsewhere.

practices.title: Returning null instead of Optional or an empty collection
practices.description: A null return forces every caller to remember a null check or risk an NPE far from the source. An empty List/Optional makes the absent case impossible to forget.
practices.risk: A caller that forgets the null check throws an NPE in production, often several layers away from where null originated.

practices.title: Returning null instead of an empty array
practices.description: Effective Java Item 54: a null array return forces every caller to add a null check that's easy to forget, mirroring the same problem as a null collection return.
practices.risk: A caller that iterates the result without a null check throws an NPE; this is especially easy to miss because arrays look like they should never be null.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: array-returning method with a null branch instead of an empty array

practices.title: String compared with == instead of .equals()
practices.description: == compares object identity, not content. Two equal strings from different sources (e.g. one from a DB read) can be == false while .equals() correctly returns true.
practices.risk: A conditional silently takes the wrong branch whenever the string wasn't interned the same way, e.g. after deserialization or string concatenation.

practices.title: Overriding equals() without hashCode() (or vice versa)
practices.description: Effective Java Item 11: equal objects must have equal hashCodes. Overriding one without the other breaks that contract.
practices.risk: The object is silently lost in a HashMap/HashSet: put() and get() with an 'equal' key can disagree on whether the entry exists, because they land in different hash buckets.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: class overrides equals() but not hashCode(), or vice versa

practices.title: Comparing floating-point numbers with ==
practices.description: Floating-point arithmetic is imprecise; two values that are mathematically equal can differ in their last bits after a computation.
practices.risk: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to false in Java, so a guard relying on exact float/double equality silently takes the wrong branch.

practices.title: == on boxed types relying on autoboxing cache
practices.description: Integer/Long caching only covers -128 to 127. Two boxed values in that range can be == true by accident, creating a false impression that == works for boxed comparison.
practices.risk: Code that 'works' in testing with small numbers (e.g. quantities 1-10) breaks in production once a real value like 1000 is compared, because it falls outside the cache range.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: == comparison between two Integer/Long-typed variables

practices.title: Closeable resource opened without try-with-resources
practices.description: A stream/connection opened without try-with-resources leaks a file handle or connection if the code between open and close throws.
practices.risk: Under load, leaked file handles or DB connections exhaust the pool and the whole service starts failing unrelated requests.

practices.title: Relying on finalize() for cleanup
practices.description: finalize() is deprecated since Java 9, runs at an unpredictable time (or never), and was never a reliable cleanup mechanism.
practices.risk: A file handle or connection 'cleaned up' only in finalize() may stay open far longer than expected, or forever if the GC never collects the object, exhausting a limited resource pool.

practices.title: Mutable HashMap shared across threads without synchronization
practices.description: HashMap is not thread-safe. Concurrent reads/writes from multiple threads can corrupt its internal structure or return stale/incorrect data.
practices.risk: Under concurrent load this can infinite-loop a thread (classic HashMap resize bug) or silently drop/return wrong entries — both hard to reproduce outside production traffic.
practices.code: private final Map<String, Session> sessions = new HashMap<>();
practices.solution: private final Map<String, Session> sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

practices.title: Swallowing InterruptedException without restoring interrupt status
practices.description: Catching InterruptedException and doing nothing (or just logging) clears the thread's interrupt flag, so code further up the call stack that checks for cancellation never finds out.
practices.risk: A thread pool shutdown or task cancellation silently fails to stop this thread's work, because the interrupt signal was absorbed and never propagated.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch (InterruptedException e) block that doesn't call Thread.currentThread().interrupt()

practices.title: Forgetting lock.unlock() in a finally block
practices.description: Unlike synchronized, an explicit Lock is not automatically released. If the code between lock() and unlock() throws, and unlock() isn't in a finally block, the lock is held forever.
practices.risk: One exception permanently deadlocks every other thread that needs the same lock, with no exception or log pointing at the actual cause.

practices.title: Calling run() instead of start() on a Thread
practices.description: run() executes the Runnable's code on the current thread, synchronously. It does not create or start a new thread — only start() does that.
practices.risk: Code that looks concurrent (spawns a Thread, calls a method on it) actually runs entirely sequentially on the calling thread; any expected parallelism silently never happens.
practices.code:
Thread t = new Thread(() -> doWork());
t.run();  // runs in the calling thread!

practices.title: Relying on Thread.stop(), Thread.suspend(), or Thread.resume()
practices.description: These methods are deprecated because they're inherently unsafe: stop() can release locks mid-update and leave shared objects in a corrupted, half-modified state.
practices.risk: A thread killed via stop() mid-write can leave a shared data structure permanently corrupted, with no exception raised to indicate anything went wrong.
practices.code:
thread.stop();
thread.suspend();
practices.solution:
thread.interrupt();
// or a higher-level construct: ExecutorService.shutdownNow(), Future.cancel()

practices.title: String concatenation in a loop
practices.description: Each += on a String allocates a new String; over N iterations this is O(n^2). StringBuilder amortizes to O(n).
practices.risk: Fine in a unit test with 5 rows, then times out or spikes latency once a real dataset with thousands of rows hits it.

practices.title: Creating unnecessary objects in a hot path
practices.description: Effective Java Item 6: creating an equivalent object repeatedly (a fresh regex Pattern, a new wrapper) when an immutable/reusable one would do wastes allocation and GC pressure for no benefit.
practices.risk: A method compiling the same regex on every call, or called in a loop over thousands of rows, spends measurable CPU time on object creation instead of the actual work.

practices.title: Using exceptions for ordinary control flow
practices.description: Effective Java Item 69: exceptions are for exceptional conditions. Using them to control a normal loop is slower than a plain condition check and obscures intent.
practices.risk: Throwing and catching an exception on every iteration of a hot loop costs orders of magnitude more than a bounds check, and confuses readers about whether the 'exceptional' path is actually expected.

practices.title: Busy-waiting with Thread.sleep() instead of proper synchronization
practices.description: Polling a condition in a sleep loop wastes CPU and reacts late (up to one sleep interval late) instead of responding the instant the condition becomes true.
practices.risk: Under load, many busy-waiting threads burn CPU that real work needs, and the artificial polling delay adds latency that a wait/notify or CompletableFuture wouldn't have.
practices.solution:
task.thenAccept(this::processResult);
// or: CountDownLatch / Object.wait()-notify() for the blocking case

practices.title: Using Vector/Hashtable/StringBuffer in single-threaded code
practices.description: These legacy classes synchronize every method call. In code that's never accessed from multiple threads, that's pure overhead with no benefit — ArrayList/HashMap/StringBuilder do the same job faster.
practices.risk: Every single-threaded call pays a lock acquisition/release cost for no reason; under profiling this shows up as unexplained synchronization overhead in a supposedly single-threaded path.
practices.code:
Vector<Order> orders = new Vector<>();
StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer();
practices.solution:
List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();

practices.title: Public mutable fields instead of encapsulation
practices.description: A public non-final field lets any caller put the object into an invalid state directly, bypassing whatever validation the class's methods would otherwise enforce.
practices.risk: Nothing stops order.status = null or an invalid value from being set directly, and the bug surfaces far from where the bad assignment happened.

practices.title: Returning a mutable internal array/collection directly from a getter
practices.description: Handing out a direct reference to an internal mutable field lets the caller modify it and corrupt the object's internal state from outside, without going through any of the class's own methods.
practices.risk: Code far away from the class silently changes its internal list (e.g. clears it), and the class has no way to detect or prevent that mutation.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: getter returns a direct reference to a mutable field instead of a copy/unmodifiable view

practices.title: Classes/members left more accessible than they need to be
practices.description: Effective Java Item 15: minimize the accessibility of every class and member. A public class or field that only needs package-private (or private) visibility becomes part of the API surface, whether that was intended or not.
practices.risk: A field or class that was never meant to be public gets used from outside its package by another team, and now can't be changed or removed without breaking them.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: public class/field with no external caller outside its own package

practices.title: No defensive copy of a mutable constructor argument
practices.description: Effective Java Item 50: storing a reference to a caller-supplied mutable object (instead of copying it) means the caller can keep a reference and mutate the 'immutable' object's internals after construction.
practices.risk: An object advertised as immutable (e.g. a date range used as a cache key) changes value after being stored, silently corrupting whatever relied on it staying constant.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: constructor stores a mutable-typed parameter (Date, array, List) without copying it

practices.title: Using raw types instead of generics
practices.description: A raw type (List instead of List<Order>) disables generic type checking entirely, deferring what should be a compile error to a runtime ClassCastException.
practices.risk: A wrong-typed element added anywhere in the codebase compiles cleanly and only fails, with a confusing ClassCastException, at the unrelated line that reads it back out.

practices.title: int constants instead of an enum
practices.description: Effective Java Item 34: the 'int enum pattern' has no type safety — any int compiles where a status is expected, valid or not.
practices.risk: orderStatus = 99 compiles fine even though 99 isn't a real status, and printing the value gives a meaningless number instead of a readable name.
practices.solution:
public enum OrderStatus { PENDING, SHIPPED }

OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.PENDING; // only valid values compile

practices.title: Ignoring compiler warnings instead of fixing them
practices.description: An unchecked or deprecation warning is the compiler telling you it found something it couldn't fully verify. Suppressing or ignoring it routinely means real bugs get waved through along with the noise.
practices.risk: A genuine unchecked-cast bug sits next to dozens of routinely-ignored warnings, indistinguishable from the noise, until it fails at runtime.

practices.title: Missing @Override on an intended override
practices.description: Without @Override, a typo'd method signature silently compiles as a brand new overload instead of failing to compile, and the intended override never runs.
practices.risk: A subclass 'overrides' equals(Object o) but actually writes equals(MyClass o) — an overload, not an override — and the superclass's equals() keeps running unnoticed.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: method named equals/hashCode/toString without an @Override annotation

practices.title: Overusing static state
practices.description: Static mutable fields are effectively global variables — shared across every caller, hard to isolate in tests, and a source of hidden coupling between unrelated code paths.
practices.risk: A test that mutates the static state leaks that change into the next test, causing flaky, order-dependent test failures that are hard to reproduce.

practices.title: instanceof/casting chains instead of polymorphism
practices.description: A growing if/else-if chain checking an object's runtime type and casting it is exactly what virtual dispatch (an overridden method) is meant to replace.
practices.risk: Every new subtype requires finding and updating every instanceof chain across the codebase; missing one is a silent bug, not a compile error.

practices.title: Long methods / God classes doing too much
practices.description: A method or class handling several unrelated responsibilities (validation, persistence, notification, formatting) is impossible to test in isolation and risky to change — every edit risks breaking an unrelated concern.
practices.risk: A one-line fix to the notification logic requires understanding and re-testing the entire method, including the unrelated persistence and validation code that method also does.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: method body exceeding roughly 80-100 lines mixing multiple unrelated responsibilities

practices.title: Deep inheritance hierarchies instead of composition
practices.description: Favoring composition ("has-a") over inheritance ("is-a") when there's no true substitutability relationship keeps a change three levels up from rippling unpredictably through every subclass.
practices.risk: A behavior change in a base class two or three levels up breaks a subclass's assumptions in a way that's hard to trace back to the actual change.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: inheritance chain deeper than 2-3 levels for a non-framework class

practices.title: Hardcoding a dependency instead of injecting it
practices.description: Effective Java Item 5: a class that constructs its own collaborator internally can't be tested with a fake/mock and can't be reconfigured without editing the class's source.
practices.risk: Writing a unit test for this class requires the real dependency (a real DB connection, a real HTTP client) to exist and work, turning a unit test into a slow, flaky integration test.

practices.title: Inheritance used for code reuse across unrelated classes
practices.description: Effective Java Item 18: extending a class purely to reuse its methods (not because of a genuine is-a relationship) couples the subclass to the superclass's implementation details, which can change underneath it.
practices.risk: A superclass method the subclass never even calls changes its internal behavior in a library upgrade, and the subclass breaks in a way nobody expected because it was never really a semantic subtype.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: class extends a concrete collection/utility class purely to add instrumentation

practices.title: A class designed for inheritance with no documentation of overridable behavior
practices.description: Effective Java Item 19: if a class permits subclassing, it must document exactly how its methods interact — or explicitly prohibit inheritance (final, or a private constructor).
practices.risk: A subclass overrides a method the base class secretly calls from its own constructor, and the override runs before the subclass's own fields are initialized, producing confusing null/zero values.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: constructor calls an overridable (non-final, non-private) instance method

practices.title: Using an abstract class where an interface would give more flexibility
practices.description: Effective Java Item 20: a class can only extend one abstract class but can implement many interfaces. Choosing an abstract class as the contract forecloses a consumer's ability to also extend something else.
practices.risk: A class that needs to satisfy this contract and also extend an unrelated base class (e.g. a framework's base class) simply can't, because Java has no multiple inheritance of classes.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: abstract class with only abstract methods and no shared state/implementation

practices.title: Using clone() to copy an object
practices.description: Object.clone() has a famously broken contract (it doesn't call constructors, interacts badly with final fields, and Cloneable carries no visible clone() method). A copy constructor or static factory is simpler and safer.
practices.risk: A subclass added later inherits a clone() that shallow-copies fields it doesn't know about, or throws CloneNotSupportedException in a place nobody expected an exception.

practices.title: Using reflection without strong justification
practices.description: Reflection bypasses normal access control and type checking, is brittle across refactors (a renamed field breaks it silently until runtime), and is significantly slower than a direct call.
practices.risk: A routine rename of a private field compiles cleanly everywhere except the reflective access, which now throws NoSuchFieldException only when that code path actually runs.

practices.title: Calling System.exit() from library or business logic
practices.description: System.exit() terminates the entire JVM immediately — not just the current request or operation. In a server, container, or test runner, that takes down every other in-flight request with it.
practices.risk: A single invalid-config check in a rarely-used code path kills the whole running application (or test suite) instead of just failing the one operation that hit it.

practices.title: Relying on the order of static initialization blocks
practices.description: Static field/block initialization order depends on declaration order within the class and load order across classes — easy to get subtly wrong and hard to see just by reading one class.
practices.risk: Reordering two unrelated-looking static declarations (or splitting a class into two files) silently changes which value a static field ends up with, with no compiler warning.
practices.solution:
// Keep static initialization simple and independent, or use lazy/explicit
// initialization instead of interdependent static blocks.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: multiple interdependent static initializer blocks in one class

practices.title: Using assert for runtime validation in production code
practices.description: Java assertions are disabled by default (the JVM needs -ea to enable them), so an assert used for business validation silently does nothing in a standard production deployment.
practices.risk: A precondition check written as `assert amount > 0` never actually runs in production, so invalid data sails straight through into logic that assumed it was checked.

practices.title: Value objects that should be immutable but aren't
practices.description: Effective Java Item 17: a value-like object (Money, DateRange, Point) with setters can be mutated by any holder, and that mutation is invisible to every other piece of code holding the same reference.
practices.risk: A Money object passed into a pricing calculation gets mutated by that calculation, and the caller's own copy silently changes value even though they never called a setter themselves.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: class with a setter for a field that conceptually represents a fixed value (money, date range, coordinate)

practices.title: Modifying a collection while iterating it with a for-each loop
practices.description: Calling list.remove()/add() on the collection itself during a for-each loop (rather than via the Iterator) throws a ConcurrentModificationException — even single-threaded.
practices.risk: Removing an item conditionally inside a for-each loop throws at runtime the moment more than one item needs removing, a bug that's easy to miss in a quick manual test with only one matching item.
practices.solution: orders.removeIf(Order::isCancelled);

practices.title: Mutating an object after it's used as a Set element or Map key
practices.description: HashSet/HashMap place an element by its hashCode() at insertion time. Changing a field that hashCode() depends on afterward moves the object logically, but not physically — it's now in the wrong bucket.
practices.risk: contains()/get() on the exact same object reference returns false/null after the mutation, because the hash-based lookup checks the new (changed) bucket while the entry still lives in the old one.
practices.solution:
// Prefer immutable objects (or records) as Set elements / Map keys,
// so there's no setter that could invalidate the hash after insertion.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: an object added to a HashSet/HashMap has a setter called on it afterward

practices.title: Ambiguous method overloads with varargs/autoboxing
practices.description: Overloads that differ only by a boxed vs. primitive type, or that mix a fixed-arity overload with a varargs one, can resolve to a different method than the author intended, silently.
practices.risk: Adding a new overload later changes which existing overload a call site resolves to, without any compile error, because overload resolution rules are subtle and easy to get wrong.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: multiple overloads of the same method name differing only in boxed/primitive or varargs form

practices.title: Telescoping constructors for many optional parameters
practices.description: Effective Java Item 2: a chain of constructors adding one more optional parameter each time forces callers to pass values they don't care about just to reach the one they need, and it's easy to swap two same-typed arguments by mistake.
practices.risk: A caller passing (10, 5, true, false) to a 4-parameter constructor swaps the two booleans without any compile error, and the bug isn't visible until the wrong behavior shows up at runtime.
practices.solution:
Pizza pizza = Pizza.builder()
    .size(12)
    .cheese(true)
    .pepperoni(false)
    .build();
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: chain of 3+ overloaded constructors each calling this(...) with one more parameter

practices.title: No Builder pattern for a class with many constructor parameters
practices.description: Effective Java Item 2: beyond roughly 4 constructor parameters (especially several of the same type), positional arguments become genuinely hard to get right at every call site.
practices.risk: Two adjacent String or int parameters get passed in the wrong order; it compiles fine and fails silently or produces subtly wrong behavior.
practices.code: new Order("user-123", "addr-1", "addr-2", true, false, 3, 19.99);
practices.solution:
Order.builder()
    .userId("user-123")
    .shippingAddress("addr-1")
    .billingAddress("addr-2")
    .giftWrap(true)
    .expedited(false)
    .quantity(3)
    .price(19.99)
    .build();
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: constructor call with 5+ positional arguments of primitive/String type

practices.title: The constant-interface antipattern
practices.description: Effective Java Item 22: an interface that exists only to declare constants leaks those constants into the public API of every class that implements it, whether or not that class wants them exposed.
practices.risk: Implementing the interface for its constants also commits every implementing class to exposing them publicly forever, and removing the constants later is a breaking change for classes that only ever wanted the behavior, not the constants.

practices.title: Declaring a variable by its implementation type instead of its interface
practices.description: Effective Java Item 64: declaring HashMap<String, Order> instead of Map<String, Order> locks every line that uses it to the concrete implementation, even though nothing about the logic actually needs it.
practices.risk: Swapping HashMap for a LinkedHashMap or a concurrent variant later requires hunting down every declared-as-HashMap variable across the codebase instead of changing one line at the construction site.
practices.code: HashMap<String, Order> ordersByUserId = new HashMap<>();
practices.solution: Map<String, Order> ordersByUserId = new HashMap<>();

practices.title: Inventing a custom exception where a standard one already fits
practices.description: Effective Java Item 72: IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, and similar standard types already cover most common error conditions. An ad hoc custom type for the same situation isn't recognized by tooling or reviewers the way the standard ones are.
practices.risk: A caller writing a catch block for the well-known IllegalArgumentException doesn't catch this class's homemade InvalidQuantityException, and the error propagates further than intended.

practices.title: Obsolete object references in a manually-managed structure
practices.description: Effective Java Item 7: popping an element off a manually-managed array-backed stack (or removing from a cache) without nulling out the reference leaves the object reachable, so the garbage collector can never reclaim it.
practices.risk: A long-running service's memory grows slowly and steadily until it OOMs, and the leak is invisible in a short-lived test because it only shows up after enough push/pop cycles accumulate.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: manual array-backed collection whose remove/pop doesn't null out the vacated slot

practices.title: Magic numbers/strings instead of named constants
practices.description: A bare literal repeated across the codebase means the meaning lives only in the author's head, and every occurrence has to be found and updated together if it changes.
practices.risk: Six months later nobody remembers what the number means, or a typo'd literal in one of the many copies silently fails to match.

practices.title: Anonymous inner class where a lambda would be clearer
practices.description: Effective Java Item 42/43: for a functional interface, a lambda is shorter and avoids the anonymous class's confusing this (which refers to the anonymous class instance, not the enclosing object).
practices.risk: Code inside an anonymous class that calls this.someField silently reads the anonymous class's own field/method instead of the enclosing object's, a mistake a lambda's lexical this doesn't allow.
practices.solution: button.setOnClickListener(v -> handleClick());

practices.title: Overly broad variable scope
practices.description: Effective Java Item 57: declaring a variable well before its first use, or reusing a loop variable name across unrelated loops, makes it easy to accidentally reference a stale value from an earlier iteration or an unrelated code path.
practices.risk: Copy-pasting a loop body and forgetting to reset a variable declared outside both loops carries a stale value from the first loop into the second, silently.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: variable declared many lines before its first actual use

practices.title: Magic strings / stringly-typed code
practices.description: Using raw string literals as pseudo-enums (a status, a role, a mode) means a typo ("Admin" vs "ADMIN") compiles fine and fails silently at runtime instead of at compile time.
practices.risk: A typo'd literal in one of several scattered comparisons silently never matches, and the resulting bug looks like a logic error rather than the actual cause: a string that doesn't quite match.
practices.code:
if ("ACTIVE".equals(user.getStatus())) { }
map.put("role", "ADMIN");
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: the same string literal used repeatedly as a status/type/mode/role discriminator

practices.title: Deeply nested if-else / switch statements
practices.description: Nesting depth beyond 3-4 levels makes it hard to hold all the active conditions in your head while reading any single branch, and each new case multiplies the number of paths to reason about.
practices.risk: A bug fix added to the innermost branch doesn't account for a condition three levels up that the author lost track of while scrolling through the nesting.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: if/switch nesting depth greater than 3-4 levels

practices.title: Multiple top-level classes in a single source file
practices.description: Effective Java Item 25: Java allows several top-level classes in one .java file, but which one 'wins' if the same class is accidentally defined in two files can depend on compilation order.
practices.risk: Two files each define a small unrelated Helper class at the top level; depending on compile order, the build silently picks one definition over the other with no error.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: more than one top-level class/interface declaration in a single .java file

practices.title: Using float/double for money or precise decimal calculations
practices.description: Binary floating-point can't represent most decimal fractions exactly, so arithmetic on float/double accumulates small rounding errors.
practices.risk: 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004; in a financial calculation these tiny errors compound across many operations into an amount that's visibly wrong at the cent level.
practices.solution:
BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("0.1").add(new BigDecimal("0.2"));
// use the String constructor, never `new BigDecimal(0.1)` (a double literal)

practices.title: Relying on implicit narrowing conversions
practices.description: Assigning a wider primitive type into a narrower one without an explicit cast silently truncates or overflows the value instead of failing to compile.
practices.risk: A value of 130 assigned into a byte silently wraps around to -126 instead of raising any error, and the bug only surfaces much later when the wrong number is used downstream.
practices.code:
int value = 130;
byte b = (byte) value;  // silent overflow, no warning that data was lost

practices.title: Preferring wrapper types over primitives in performance-sensitive code
practices.description: Boxing/unboxing a wrapper type (Integer, Long) on every loop iteration allocates an object where a primitive needs none, and introduces an unboxing NullPointerException risk that a primitive can't have.
practices.risk: A List<Integer> summed via a for-each loop silently throws an NPE the day one element happens to be null, in code that looks identical to summing a primitive array.
practices.solution:
int sum = list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
// or filter nulls first if they're expected: list.stream().filter(Objects::nonNull)...

practices.title: Using Boolean wrapper when a primitive boolean would do
practices.description: A Boolean field defaults to null (not false), which throws a NullPointerException the moment it's auto-unboxed into a primitive boolean context.
practices.risk: A newly-added Boolean field that's never explicitly initialized is null until set, and the first isActive() call on a fresh object throws an NPE instead of returning false.

practices.title: Missing input validation on a public method
practices.description: A public method that uses its parameters without checking them pushes the burden of correctness onto every caller, forever, instead of failing fast at the boundary.
practices.risk: A null or out-of-range value passed in from three call sites away isn't caught here; it propagates further into the system and fails with a confusing error far from where the bad value actually originated.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: public method using its parameters with no null/range/blank checks

practices.title: Using System.out.println/e.printStackTrace() instead of a logger
practices.description: Console output has no log levels, no structured fields, and can't be routed, filtered, or aggregated the way a real logging framework's output can.
practices.risk: In production, this output either goes nowhere useful (no console attached) or floods stdout with no way to filter it by severity when investigating an incident.

practices.title: Logging and rethrowing the same exception
practices.description: Logging an exception and then rethrowing it means the same stack trace gets logged again by whatever catches it further up, duplicating noise in the logs for a single failure.
practices.risk: An incident investigation finds the same error logged three times at three layers, making it unclear whether this was one failure or three separate ones.

practices.title: Incorrect log levels
practices.description: Logging routine, expected events at ERROR (or genuine failures at INFO/DEBUG) makes logs either too noisy to scan for real problems or hides the real problems entirely.
practices.risk: An on-call engineer's ERROR-level alert channel is full of routine page views, so a real production failure logged at the wrong level goes unnoticed alongside the noise.
practices.code:
log.error("User {} viewed page {}", userId, page);  // not an error
log.info("NullPointerException occurred", e);  // hides a real failure
practices.solution:
log.debug("User {} viewed page {}", userId, page);
log.error("Failed to process order", e);
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: business-as-usual event logged at ERROR, or an exception logged at INFO/DEBUG

practices.title: Ignoring the result of an immutable String method
practices.description: String is immutable — trim(), toUpperCase(), replace(), etc. all return a new String and leave the original unchanged. Calling one without using its return value does nothing.
practices.risk: Code that calls name.trim() expecting it to clean up name in place silently has no effect at all; the untrimmed value flows through unchanged.
practices.solution:
String name = "  Alice  ";
name = name.trim().toUpperCase();

practices.title: Misusing String.intern() on unbounded input
practices.description: intern() adds a string to the JVM's string pool, which lives for the life of the application. Interning strings derived from unbounded user input can grow that pool without limit.
practices.risk: Interning every distinct value of a high-cardinality user-supplied field (e.g. a search query) slowly grows memory that's never reclaimed, until the application runs out of heap.
practices.code: String s = userInput.intern();  // dangerous with unbounded/high-cardinality input
practices.solution:
// Avoid intern() outside a small, fixed, well-understood set of strings.
String s = userInput;

practices.title: Relying on the default platform charset
practices.description: String.getBytes() and new String(byte[]) without an explicit charset use the JVM's default platform charset, which differs across operating systems and JVM configurations.
practices.risk: Code that encodes/decodes text correctly in local development (UTF-8 by default) corrupts non-ASCII characters when it runs on a server or container with a different default charset.
practices.code:
byte[] bytes = str.getBytes();               // uses default charset
String s = new String(bytes);                // same problem
practices.solution:
byte[] bytes = str.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
String s = new String(bytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

practices.title: Using new String("literal")
practices.description: A string literal is already interned and shared. Wrapping it in `new String(...)` creates a redundant duplicate object and opts out of the string pool for no benefit.
practices.risk: No functional bug, but every occurrence allocates an unnecessary object; at scale in a hot path this adds needless GC pressure for zero benefit.
practices.code: String s = new String("hello");
practices.solution: String s = "hello";

practices.title: Using Calendar/Date instead of the java.time API
practices.description: java.util.Date and Calendar are mutable, use confusing zero-based months, and have a long history of subtly wrong behavior around time zones and DST. java.time (Java 8+) fixes all of this with immutable, well-designed types.
practices.risk: A Calendar passed between two pieces of code gets mutated by one of them (calendar.add(...) mutates in place), and the other silently sees a different date than it expected.
practices.solution:
LocalDate date = LocalDate.now().plusDays(7);
// or Instant / ZonedDateTime depending on whether a time zone matters

practices.title: Creating a new SimpleDateFormat per call, or sharing one across threads
practices.description: SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe — sharing one instance across threads corrupts its internal state, while creating a fresh one on every call wastes the (non-trivial) construction cost.
practices.risk: Two threads formatting dates through the same shared SimpleDateFormat at the same time can get back a mangled, wrong-looking date string with no exception thrown — just silently corrupted output.

practices.title: Ignoring the return value of a method that signals success/failure
practices.description: Methods like File.delete(), File.mkdirs(), or Collection.remove() return a boolean indicating whether the operation actually happened. Ignoring it treats a silent failure as if it succeeded.
practices.risk: A cleanup job that calls file.delete() without checking the result reports success even when the file was locked and never actually got deleted, masking a real operational problem.
practices.code:
file.delete();     // return value ignored
file.mkdirs();     // same

practices.title: Comparable.compareTo() inconsistent with equals()
practices.description: If compareTo() returns 0 for two objects that equals() says are not equal (or vice versa), sorted collections like TreeSet/TreeMap silently drop or misplace entries, because they use compareTo() for identity, not equals().
practices.risk: Adding an object to a TreeSet silently does nothing (or replaces an existing element) if its compareTo() considers it equal to something already in the set, even when equals() says they're different objects.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: compareTo() implementation that compares a different set of fields than equals()

practices.title: Comparing classes with getClass() == instead of instanceof
practices.description: obj.getClass() == MyClass.class fails for any subclass or dynamic proxy (common with Hibernate, Spring AOP, and many mocking frameworks), even when the object genuinely satisfies an instanceof check.
practices.risk: An entity loaded as a Hibernate lazy proxy fails a getClass()-based equals()/type check that would have passed with instanceof, causing a spurious 'not equal' or 'wrong type' result purely because of the proxy wrapper.
practices.code: if (obj.getClass() == MyClass.class) { }
practices.solution:
if (obj instanceof MyClass) { }
// or, with pattern matching: if (obj instanceof MyClass my) { }

practices.title: Field injection instead of constructor injection
practices.description: @Autowired on a field hides the dependency from the constructor signature, makes the class harder to unit test without Spring, and allows constructing an object in an invalid half-wired state.
practices.risk: A missing dependency isn't caught until Spring wires it at runtime (or a plain `new` in a test leaves it null), instead of failing to compile/construct.
practices.code:
@Autowired
private OrderService orderService;

practices.title: Unnecessary @Autowired on a bean's single constructor
practices.description: Since Spring 4.3, a class with exactly one constructor is auto-wired by Spring without needing @Autowired on it. Adding it anyway is harmless but purely visual noise every reader has to see past.
practices.risk: No functional risk, but it invites the belief that @Autowired is required there, and someone copies the pattern onto a class with multiple constructors where it actually matters which one gets picked.

practices.title: Using new to manually create a Spring-managed bean
practices.description: Constructing a @Service/@Component/@Repository class with `new` bypasses the Spring container entirely — no dependency injection into it, and none of Spring's proxies (transactions, security, AOP) apply to it.
practices.risk: A manually-`new`'d service silently runs without @Transactional taking effect, so a multi-step write that should roll back on failure doesn't, because there's no Spring transaction proxy wrapping this instance.
practices.code:
OrderService service = new OrderService();
service.createOrder(order);

practices.title: Returning a JPA entity directly from a REST controller
practices.description: Serializing the entity couples the wire format to the DB schema, risks leaking fields (e.g. an internal audit column) that were never meant to be public, and can trigger lazy-loading exceptions outside a transaction.
practices.risk: Adding an internal-only DB column silently exposes it in the API response; a lazy collection accessed by the serializer outside the transaction throws LazyInitializationException in production.

practices.title: Missing @Transactional on a multi-step write
practices.description: Without @Transactional, a failure partway through a multi-step write (e.g. debit one account, credit another) leaves the database in an inconsistent, partially-applied state.
practices.risk: A crash between the two writes leaves money debited from one account and never credited to the other, with no automatic rollback.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: multi-repository-write method body without a @Transactional on the enclosing method

practices.title: Stateful Spring beans (mutable fields shared across requests)
practices.description: A @Service/@Component bean is a singleton by default — one instance shared by every request. A mutable instance field on it is shared, unsynchronized state across every concurrent user.
practices.risk: Two users hitting the same endpoint at the same time see each other's data: one user's cart items appear in another user's session, because both requests mutate the exact same shared list.

practices.title: Hardcoding configuration values instead of externalizing them
practices.description: A URL, timeout, or port baked directly into Java source requires a full rebuild and redeploy to change, and can't differ between dev/staging/prod without maintaining separate code branches.
practices.risk: Rotating a third-party API's URL (a routine operational change) requires a code change, code review, and full deployment pipeline instead of an environment variable update.
practices.code:
private String apiUrl = "https://api.example.com/v1";
private int timeout = 5000;

practices.title: Storing secrets in application.yml committed to Git
practices.description: A plaintext password or API key in a properties/YAML file checked into version control is exposed to everyone with repo access, and stays in git history even after being 'removed' in a later commit.
practices.risk: Anyone who ever had read access to the repository — including in its history — can extract and use the credential; rotating it is the only real fix once this has happened.
practices.code:
spring:
  datasource:
    password: MySuperSecretPassword123
practices.solution:
spring:
  datasource:
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
# supplied via environment variable, Vault, or a secrets manager — never committed

practices.title: Missing @Valid on a REST request body
practices.description: @RequestBody without @Valid deserializes the JSON into the object but never runs the bean-validation constraints (@NotNull, @Size, etc.) declared on it, so invalid data reaches business logic unchecked.
practices.risk: A request missing a required field, or with a negative quantity, passes straight through the controller and fails later inside business logic with a much less specific, harder-to-debug error.

practices.title: N+1 query from a lazily-loaded association accessed in a loop
practices.description: Accessing a lazy @OneToMany/@ManyToOne inside a loop over the parent entities issues one extra query per row instead of a single joined/batched fetch.
practices.risk: A page that's fast with 10 test rows issues hundreds of queries against real data and times out or saturates the connection pool.
practices.solution:
@Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer")
List<Order> findAllWithCustomer();
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: loop over a repository result accessing a lazy association's getter

practices.title: Loading an entire table into memory instead of paging
practices.description: findAll() with no Pageable pulls every row into memory and serializes all of it, regardless of what the caller actually needed.
practices.risk: Works in dev with 50 rows, then OOMs or produces a multi-second, multi-megabyte response once the table has millions.

practices.title: Missing @Version field allows lost updates
practices.description: Without optimistic locking, two concurrent updates to the same row both succeed, and the second silently overwrites the first's changes.
practices.risk: Two users editing the same order at once: one user's changes vanish with no error and no record that a conflict happened.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: @Entity class with mutable fields and no @Version

practices.title: SQL built via string concatenation
practices.description: Concatenating a user-controlled value into a SQL string is a SQL injection vector. A PreparedStatement with bound parameters is not optional here, even for internal tools.
practices.risk: An attacker-controlled userId value like `' OR '1'='1` returns every row in the table, or worse, chains into a destructive statement.

practices.title: Missing index on a frequently filtered or joined column
practices.description: A WHERE/JOIN on a column with no index forces a full table scan; the query gets slower in direct proportion to table size.
practices.risk: A query that returns in milliseconds on a 1,000-row dev table takes seconds on the 10-million-row production table, and locks up under concurrent load.
practices.solution:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders(customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: WHERE/JOIN column with no matching CREATE INDEX in the migration set

practices.title: Table charset not set to utf8mb4
practices.description: MySQL's utf8 charset is actually a 3-byte-max encoding and can't store emoji or many CJK/astral characters; utf8mb4 is the real UTF-8.
practices.risk: Saving a name or comment containing an emoji either throws an 'Incorrect string value' error or silently truncates the string at the offending character.

practices.title: Comparing a VARCHAR column to a number causes an implicit cast and a full table scan
practices.description: MySQL implicitly converts types in a comparison. WHERE order_code = 12345 against a VARCHAR column silently casts every row's value instead of using the index.
practices.risk: A query that should hit an index on order_code instead scans the whole table, and this only shows up once the table is large enough to notice.
practices.code: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_code = 12345;
practices.solution: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_code = '12345';

practices.title: Loose equality (==) instead of strict equality (===)
practices.description: == performs type coercion before comparing (0 == '' is true, null == undefined is true), producing comparisons that pass when they shouldn't.
practices.risk: A guard like `if (userId == 0)` also matches an empty string or false, letting an unintended branch execute for unexpected input shapes.

practices.title: var instead of let/const causing function-scoped leakage
practices.description: var is function-scoped and hoisted, so a variable declared inside a block (loop, if) leaks outside it and can be redeclared without error — unlike the block-scoped let/const.
practices.risk: A classic bug: a var loop counter captured in an async callback ends up with the same final value in every callback instead of each iteration's value.

practices.title: Using any to silence a type error instead of typing the value
practices.description: any opts a value out of type checking entirely, so a typo'd property name or wrong argument type compiles cleanly and fails only at runtime.
practices.risk: A refactor that renames a field breaks every `any`-typed call site silently at compile time; the failure only shows up when that code path runs.

practices.title: Mutating state directly instead of via the state setter
practices.description: React decides whether to re-render by comparing references. Mutating an array/object in place keeps the same reference, so React doesn't know anything changed.
practices.risk: The UI silently stops reflecting the actual data — an item added to a list never appears until some unrelated state change forces a re-render.

practices.title: dangerouslySetInnerHTML with unsanitized content
practices.description: Rendering raw HTML from an untrusted source (user input, an external API) without sanitizing it first is a stored/reflected XSS vector.
practices.risk: A user-submitted comment containing a <script> tag executes in every other visitor's browser session, with access to their cookies/tokens.
practices.code: <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: comment.body }} />
practices.solution:
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';

<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.body) }} />

practices.title: Inline function/object literal passed as a prop defeats React.memo
practices.description: A new function or object literal is created on every render. Passed to a React.memo'd child, it breaks the prop-equality check that memo relies on, so the child re-renders anyway.
practices.risk: A list of memoized rows re-renders on every parent state change regardless of the memoization, and nobody notices why the optimization isn't working.
practices.code: <MemoizedRow onSelect={() => handleSelect(item.id)} style={{ padding: 8 }} />

practices.title: Non-semantic clickable div instead of a button element
practices.description: A <div onClick> gets none of a <button>'s built-in keyboard focus, Enter/Space activation, or screen-reader role for free — all of it has to be reimplemented by hand, and usually isn't.
practices.risk: A keyboard-only or screen-reader user cannot activate the control at all; it's invisible to assistive technology as an interactive element.
practices.code: Submit
practices.solution: <button type="button" className="submit-btn" onClick={handleSubmit}>Submit</button>

practices.title: Image missing alt text
practices.description: An with no alt attribute is announced by a screen reader as just the filename, or skipped entirely, conveying nothing about its content or purpose.
practices.risk: A screen-reader user gets no information about a meaningful image (a chart, a product photo) and may miss content sighted users rely on.

practices.title: Overusing !important instead of fixing selector specificity
practices.description: !important overrides normal cascade rules and compounds: once one rule needs it to win, the next override needs !important too, and the cascade becomes unpredictable.
practices.risk: A later, more specific rule that should win silently loses to an unrelated !important declared months earlier, and the fix is to add yet another !important.

practices.title: Hardcoded magic-number colors/spacing instead of design tokens
practices.description: A literal hex color or pixel value repeated across many rules means a design change requires a find-and-replace across the whole codebase instead of one variable update.
practices.risk: A brand color update or a spacing-scale change requires touching dozens of files, and it's easy to miss one, leaving a visibly inconsistent UI.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: repeated literal color/spacing value across multiple rules with no custom property

practices.title: Overriding Bootstrap classes with inline !important instead of Sass variable overrides
practices.description: Patching Bootstrap's look with scattered inline !important styles fights the framework instead of configuring it, and breaks the next time Bootstrap is upgraded.
practices.risk: A Bootstrap version bump changes a selector's specificity and the !important overrides stop applying in some places but not others, producing inconsistent styling that's hard to trace.
practices.code: <button class="btn btn-primary" style="background-color: #123456 !important;">Save</button>

practices.title: Hardcoding pixel breakpoints instead of Bootstrap's responsive grid/utilities
practices.description: A custom @media (max-width: 800px) duplicates logic Bootstrap's grid and responsive utility classes (col-md-*, d-none d-md-block) already provide consistently across the app.
practices.risk: Every hand-rolled breakpoint is a slightly different number, so the app's responsive behavior becomes inconsistent page to page, and Bootstrap's own components break out of sync with the custom ones.
practices.solution: ...

practices.title: Hardcoded credential or API key in source
practices.description: A committed secret is compromised the moment it's pushed, whether or not the repo is public today — history doesn't forget. Load secrets from environment/config at runtime instead.
practices.risk: Anyone with read access to the repo (or its history, even after a later 'fix') can extract and use the credential; rotation is the only real remediation once this happens.
practices.code: String apiKey = "sk-live-91a2b3c4d5e6f7g8h9i0";
practices.solution: String apiKey = System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY");

practices.title: API key or secret embedded in a frontend bundle
practices.description: Anything shipped in client-side JavaScript is visible to every visitor via browser devtools, regardless of minification. A frontend can only safely hold public, purpose-limited keys.
practices.risk: A backend-scoped API key embedded for convenience gets extracted from the bundle and used directly against the provider, outside any of the app's own rate limits or authorization checks.
practices.code:
const OPENAI_KEY = "sk-live-91a2b3c4d5e6f7g8h9i0";
fetch("https://api.openai.com/v1/...", { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${OPENAI_KEY}` } });
practices.solution:
// Call your own backend, which holds the real key server-side.
fetch("/api/reviews", { method: "POST", body });

practices.title: Logging sensitive data
practices.description: Passwords, tokens, and full card numbers written to logs end up in log aggregators, backups, and support tickets — systems with far weaker access control than the original request.
practices.risk: A support engineer or a compromised log-aggregation account gets direct access to live credentials, without ever touching the production database.
practices.code: log.info("Login attempt: user={} password={}", username, password);
practices.solution: log.info("Login attempt: user={}", username);

practices.title: Adding a dependency without pinning a version or verifying the package name
practices.description: An unpinned version range can pull in a breaking or malicious update on the next build; a mistyped package name can pull in an unrelated (or malicious, typosquatted) package entirely.
practices.risk: A typosquatted package (e.g. `reqeusts` instead of `requests`) runs arbitrary code at install time; an unpinned range silently upgrades into a breaking API change on the next clean install.
practices.code: "some-utility": "*"
practices.solution: "some-utility": "^2.3.1"  // verified on npmjs.com: correct name, real maintainers, matches expected download counts
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: dependency manifest entry with a wildcard/unbounded version range

practices.title: Test with no assertions
practices.description: A test that only calls the method under test and returns proves the code doesn't throw — nothing about whether it did the right thing. It stays green through real regressions.
practices.risk: A genuine regression in business logic ships to production with full test coverage reported green, because the test never actually checked the outcome.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ASSERTION_HEURISTIC: method annotated @Test whose body contains no assert*/verify* call
